title: Does hiring a property manager affect the short-term rental tax loophole?
excerpt: A paid manager rules out most of the IRS material participation tests that the short-term rental exception depends on. Which tests survive, what counts as hours, and the options owners have.

seo.title: Property Managers and the STR Tax Loophole (2026)
seo.description: Hiring a property manager can end material participation for the short-term rental tax loophole. The IRS tests, the 500-hour route and what counts, 2026.

heroCaption: Hours spent running a short-term rental, not just owning it, decide whether its losses can offset W-2 income.
bodyHtml:
Owners who use the short-term rental exception to offset W-2 income with rental losses often ask the same question before hiring a property manager: will a manager cost them the tax treatment? Under the IRS material participation rules, it can. A full-service manager makes two of the seven tests close to unreachable, and a third much harder. This guide explains which tests survive, what the IRS counts as participation, and the options owners have.

As of November 2026

Rules quoted from IRS Publication 925 (for 2025 returns) and Treasury Regulation 1.469-5T as published in November 2026.

What is the short-term rental tax loophole?

It is a combination of two rules. First, according to IRS Publication 925, an activity is not a rental activity if "the average period of customer use of the property is 7 days or less." Second, the owner must materially participate. When both apply, losses (often enlarged by a cost segregation study) are not passive and can offset wages and other active income. Our earlier guide to the 7-day rule covers the first half; this one covers the second.

The average is figured by dividing the total days in all rental periods by the number of rentals during the tax year. Hiring a manager does not change that math. It changes the participation half.

What are the seven material participation tests?

The IRS treats an owner as materially participating for the year if any one of seven tests in Publication 925 is met. Three matter for most short-term rental owners: more than 500 hours; substantially all the participation of everyone involved; or more than 100 hours and at least as much as any other individual. The other four cover prior-year history, personal service businesses and a facts-and-circumstances test.

The full list, as Publication 925 states it:

  • Test 1: more than 500 hours of participation during the year.
  • Test 2: your participation was substantially all the participation of all individuals, including people with no ownership interest.
  • Test 3: more than 100 hours, and at least as much as any other individual, including people with no ownership interest.
  • Test 4: the activity is a significant participation activity and your significant participation activities total more than 500 hours.
  • Test 5: you materially participated in any 5 of the 10 preceding tax years.
  • Test 6: a personal service activity in which you materially participated in any 3 preceding years.
  • Test 7: based on all the facts and circumstances, regular, continuous and substantial participation during the year.

Which tests does a full-service manager rule out?

Usually Tests 2, 3 and 7. A full-service manager's staff handle guest messaging, cleaning, inspections and repairs, so the owner's hours are rarely "substantially all" of the work (Test 2) or more than every other individual's (Test 3). Test 7 is closed by its own wording once a manager is paid.

Test 3: the "any other individual" comparison

Test 3 compares the owner with each other person who works on the property, not with the management company as a whole. A housekeeper who spends 150 hours a year on turnovers outworks an owner with 120 hours, and the test fails. With frequent turnovers, which is what a 7-day average implies, cleaning hours alone often pass 100.

Test 7: the management services rule

Publication 925 says an owner's time spent managing the activity does not count toward Test 7 if "any person other than you received compensation for managing the activity," or if any individual spent more hours managing it than the owner did. Treasury Regulation 1.469-5T(b)(2)(ii) sets out the same rule. A paid manager triggers the first condition by definition.

Can an owner with a manager still qualify?

Yes, through Test 1. More than 500 hours qualifies regardless of how many hours the manager or cleaners log. That is roughly 10 hours a week, and the hours must be real participation in operating the property, documented, and not investor-type work.

Three rules decide what counts:

  • Investor work is excluded. Reviewing statements, monitoring operations or analyzing finances does not count "unless you're directly involved in the day-to-day management or operations of the activity," per Publication 925.
  • A spouse's hours count. Publication 925 includes a spouse's participation even if the spouse owns no interest and the couple files separately.
  • Proof can be reasonable, not perfect. Daily time logs are not required. The IRS accepts an appointment book, calendar or narrative summary showing the services performed and approximate hours.

A second route is a narrower arrangement where the owner runs most of the operation and hires help for specific tasks. If no single person, including each cleaner, works more hours than the owner and the owner passes 100, Test 3 can still be met. That only works when the owner is the most active person on the property.

What happens if the owner does not materially participate?

The losses become passive. They can offset passive income, such as profit from other rentals, and unused passive losses carry forward to later years. Publication 925 also allows suspended losses in full when the owner disposes of the entire interest in a fully taxable transaction. The deductions are deferred, not lost, but they no longer reduce W-2 income in the year they occur.

For many owners that is an acceptable trade. The decision comes down to how much a current-year deduction is worth against the hours required to earn it, and what the home earns under each arrangement.

How should owners decide?

Start with numbers from a CPA: the size of the expected loss, the owner's marginal rate, and what deferring the loss costs. Then compare that figure with an honest count of available hours. Owners who cannot commit more than 500 documented hours, or who would not be the most active person on the property, should plan on passive treatment.
